title: Matthew 25:1–13
context: Still answering the disciples’ watchfulness questions from chapter 24, Jesus pictures the kingdom as ten virgins awaiting a delayed bridegroom. Wisdom and folly turn on oil ready before the midnight cry; those prepared enter the feast, the door shuts, and the refrain returns: watch, for you don’t know the day nor the hour.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: What earlier interpreters on each side wrote about Matthew 25:1–13.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Then shall the kingdom of heaven - That is, the candidates for it, be like ten virgins - The bridemaids on the wedding night were wont to go to the house where the bride was, with burning lamps or torches in their hands, to wait for the bride groom's coming. When he drew near, they went to meet him with their lamps, and to conduct him to the bride.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 25:1–13)

reformed.quote: By this term is meant the condition of the future Church, which was to be collected by the authority and direction of Christ. He employs this remarkable title, that believers may not deceive themselves by an erroneous opinion that they have arrived at absolute perfection.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 25:1–13)

verses.text: “Then the Kingdom of Heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom.
verses.arminianNotes:
The kingdom is likened to ten virgins going out to meet the bridegroom—shared anticipation, shared lamps.

Grace invites many into the waiting people. The issue will not be whether they started out, but whether they remain ready when He comes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jesus opens with a kingdom simile: virgins, lamps, bridegroom. The church’s posture is expectant meeting, not casual drift.

Christ sets the scene of His own return. Belonging to the wedding party is privilege under the Bridegroom’s timeline.

verses.text: Five of them were foolish, and five were wise.
verses.arminianNotes:
The split is moral and spiritual, not social: five foolish, five wise.

The passage carries a fork in the road. Grace enables wisdom; folly is a resistible path within the same company of waiters.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jesus divides the company before the delay is told. Wisdom and folly are already present among those who look alike.

Outward association with the bridegroom’s people is not the same as saving readiness. God alone finally sorts wise from foolish.

verses.text: Those who were foolish, when they took their lamps, took no oil with them,
verses.arminianNotes:
Foolishness shows in omission: lamps without oil. The foolish virgins have the outward form but no reserve.

Profession without the Spirit’s sustaining grace leaves the lamp empty. Take oil seriously while dealers are still open.
verses.reformedNotes:
The foolish take lamps yet skip oil—appearance without provision.

Empty religion can carry religious gear and still lack what the night requires. God exposes counterfeit preparation.

verses.text: but the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps.
verses.arminianNotes:
The wise bring flasks with the lamps—forethought matching hope.

Grace trains wise readiness. Oil is not earned cleverness; it is received provision for a long wait.
verses.reformedNotes:
Wisdom packs oil with the lamp. Hope plans for delay under the master’s timing.

God supplies what perseverance needs. The wise are not self-made; they are kept ready.

verses.text: Now while the bridegroom delayed, they all slumbered and slept.
verses.arminianNotes:
Delay comes; all grow drowsy and sleep—wise and foolish alike feel the wait.

Waiting is hard. Grace does not deny weariness; it keeps oil present even when eyes close.
verses.reformedNotes:
The bridegroom’s delay tests the company. Sleep falls on both groups.

Providence includes delay. The difference is not who never tires, but who already carries oil.

verses.text: But at midnight there was a cry, ‘Behold! The bridegroom is coming! Come out to meet him!’
verses.arminianNotes:
Midnight cry: the bridegroom is here—come out to meet him. Sudden summons after long quiet.

The cry still lands as a genuine call. Live ready so the announcement is joy, not scramble.
verses.reformedNotes:
The cry cuts the night. Hidden timing becomes public arrival.

The bridegroom’s hour is His. The church lives between promise and cry.

verses.text: Then all those virgins arose, and trimmed their lamps.
verses.arminianNotes:
All rise and trim lamps—shared scramble at the announcement.

Activity at the last moment differs from oil stored earlier. Trimming cannot invent what was never carried.
verses.reformedNotes:
Trimming is the common response; oil is not.

Crisis religion looks busy. Only prior provision meets the bridegroom.

verses.text: The foolish said to the wise, ‘Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The foolish beg oil from the wise—lamps going out expose emptiness.

Borrowed faith cannot substitute for one’s own trust. Ask dealers now; do not wait to borrow at midnight.
verses.reformedNotes:
Going-out lamps reveal the lack. The request admits crisis too late.

Saving readiness is not transferable stock. Each servant answers for the oil entrusted.

verses.text: But the wise answered, saying, ‘What if there isn’t enough for us and you? You go rather to those who sell, and buy for yourselves.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The wise refuse a share that would empty both; they point to the dealers.

Some helps cannot be lent at the door. Grace still points the empty-handed to the only place oil is sold—before the feast begins.
verses.reformedNotes:
Not enough for us and you—honesty, not cruelty. Dealers, not last-second transfer.

The wise cannot become oil for the foolish. Personal faith and Spirit-wrought readiness are not poolable at the threshold.

verses.text: While they went away to buy, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went in with him to the wedding feast, and the door was shut.
verses.arminianNotes:
While they buy, the bridegroom comes; the ready enter; the door shuts.

Opportunity has an end. The shut door is meant to wake hearers while it is still day.
verses.reformedNotes:
Readiness enters; delay-shopping misses the feast. The shut door is the Master’s act.

Christ’s timing closes the invitation on His terms. Being found ready is the only safe place.
verses.keyContrast: Both treat the shut door at face value. Arminians stress a sincere warning that summons present readiness; Reformed interpreters usually stress the Bridegroom’s sovereign hour that separates the prepared from the unprepared.

verses.text: Afterward the other virgins also came, saying, ‘Lord, Lord, open to us.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Late knocks and ‘Lord, lord’—religious speech after exclusion.

Words alone do not reopen what readiness would have entered. Come while the door is open.
verses.reformedNotes:
Afterward is too late. ‘Lord, lord’ without prior readiness fails.

Reformed echo of Matthew 7: confession without known relationship is empty at the door.

verses.text: But he answered, ‘Most certainly I tell you, I don’t know you.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The answer is devastating: ‘I don’t know you.’

Classical Arminians refuse to soften this: the Bridegroom’s knowledge is relational, not merely census. Grace still pleads—be known by Him now.
verses.reformedNotes:
Truly—I don’t know you. Recognition, not résumé, decides entry.

Christ’s knowledge of His own is decisive. The warning guards false assurance.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear: entrance turns on being known by the Lord. Arminians typically press an enabled, personal response of ongoing readiness; Reformed Christians highlight Christ’s effectual knowledge of His people and the impossibility of last-minute counterfeit oil.

verses.text: Watch therefore, for you don’t know the day nor the hour in which the Son of Man is coming.
verses.arminianNotes:
Watch—because day and hour remain unknown.

Watching is active faithfulness, not anxiety. Grace sustains oil until He comes.
verses.reformedNotes:
The parable lands in the same command as chapter 24: watch.

Unknown timing is God’s gift to keep the church awake. Readiness is the wise response to a certain bridegroom and an unrevealed hour.
